topics.title: 30.1 RAID
topics.summary: RAID combines devices according to a layout that trades capacity, performance, and selected failure tolerance. RAID 0 stripes without redundancy. RAID 1 mirrors. Parity-based and combined layouts offer other tradeoffs, with behavior depending on implementation and workload.

blocks.text: RAID combines devices according to a layout that trades capacity, performance, and selected failure tolerance. RAID 0 stripes without redundancy. RAID 1 mirrors. Parity-based and combined layouts offer other tradeoffs, with behavior depending on implementation and workload.

RAID is not backup. It may keep data available after a member fails, but it can preserve an accidental deletion or corruption just as faithfully as a correct write. Controllers, firmware, power, and administration can also create shared failure domains.

Plan rebuild time and degraded performance. The array’s risk during reconstruction depends on device health, workload, layout, and other factors. Test monitoring and replacement procedures rather than assuming a redundant label means no operator action is required.
Linux example — 30.1
Inspect software RAID state.

cat /proc/mdstat
lsblk -o NAME,TYPE,SIZE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINTS

blocks.text: What to check: An array's redundancy mode and actual member health require separate checks.

blocks.text: Multipath storage provides more than one path to the same logical storage device. It addresses path availability and sometimes path selection or balancing; it does not create independent copies of the data.

A crucial distinction is identity: several visible devices can represent one LUN through different paths. Formatting each apparent device separately would be catastrophic. Use the supported multipath map and stable identifiers, not an arbitrary /dev/sdX path.

Inspect with the platform’s approved multipath tooling, commonly multipath -ll, and correlate path health with the storage fabric. Queueing policy during total path loss has application consequences. Choose it with the storage owner rather than copying a generic “never fail I/O” configuration. (R65)
Linux example — 30.3
Inspect configured multipath maps.
sudo multipath -ll

topics.title: 30.4 Network Bonding
topics.summary: Bonding combines network interfaces into a logical link according to a selected mode. Active-backup focuses on failover; 802.3ad aggregation requires compatible switch configuration and distributes traffic under its hashing behavior.

cards.question: What should you check after this section’s example?
cards.code:
find /proc/net/bonding -maxdepth 1 -type f -print
# For a verified bond:
# cat /proc/net/bonding/bond0
cards.answer: Bonding mode, partner configuration, and path failure behavior must agree.

blocks.text: Bonding combines network interfaces into a logical link according to a selected mode. Active-backup focuses on failover; 802.3ad aggregation requires compatible switch configuration and distributes traffic under its hashing behavior.

Two physical links do not automatically double the throughput of one connection. The selected mode, flow hashing, peer support, and shared upstream limits determine the result. A misconfigured bond can disrupt the only management path.

Plan with the network team and use the distribution’s persistent network manager. Verify link failure and restoration from console access in a lab. Inspect the bond’s state and counters, not merely whether both cables are connected. (R65)

# For a verified bond:
# cat /proc/net/bonding/bond0

blocks.text: A bridge forwards Layer 2 frames among attached interfaces. It is useful for virtual networks and other designs where participants share a link-layer domain. It is not the same as IP routing or NAT.

Creating a bridge can change where the host’s IP configuration belongs. Moving a management interface into a bridge without transferring the intended address and route can disconnect administration. Loops and spanning-tree behavior also matter in a real switched network.

Use read-only inspection such as ip link show type bridge and bridge link before planning a change. Do not attach an untrusted lab network to an organizational network merely to make a guest reachable.

blocks.text: Tuning changes a measured behavior through a supported control. Begin with a baseline and a hypothesis connecting the setting to the bottleneck. Record the original value, test workload, expected improvement, side effects, and rollback.

Do not deploy collections of unexplained sysctls because they contain technical-looking names. Queue lengths, cache behavior, network buffers, and scheduler settings trade resources and latency in workload-dependent ways.

Promote a successful experiment into persistent configuration only after functional, security, and recovery tests. Revisit it after kernel and workload changes. A historical exception can become harmful when the assumptions that justified it no longer hold.

topics.title: 30.8 Resource Controls
topics.summary: systemd can apply cgroup policies such as CPU weighting, CPU quotas, memory thresholds, and task-count limits. Relative weighting influences competition; a hard ceiling limits a workload even when other resources may be idle.

cards.question: What should you check after this section’s example?
cards.answer: Values may be unlimited; compare limits with measured workload and parent-scope policy.

blocks.text: systemd can apply cgroup policies such as CPU weighting, CPU quotas, memory thresholds, and task-count limits. Relative weighting influences competition; a hard ceiling limits a workload even when other resources may be idle.
An illustrative drop-in for a lab service is:

[Service]
CPUWeight=50
MemoryHigh=192M
MemoryMax=256M
TasksMax=64
blocks.title: Original Linux example

blocks.text: These are example values, not production sizing recommendations. MemoryHigh and MemoryMax have different pressure and enforcement roles. Check installed support and actual workload behavior. A service needing more memory may fail under this ceiling by design. (R16, R19)

Use systemctl edit or a managed drop-in, reload the manager, and apply the change under the service’s supported lifecycle. Record whether the selected property changes live or needs a restart, then inspect the effective values and test failure handling.
Linux example — 30.8
Inspect an existing service's cgroup controls.
systemctl show nginx.service -p ControlGroup -p MemoryMax -p CPUQuotaPerSecUSec -p TasksMax

blocks.text: Larger memory pages can reduce address-translation overhead for some workloads. Explicit HugeTLB pages and Transparent Huge Pages are different mechanisms with different allocation and management behavior.

Reserved HugeTLB memory is not freely available for every other allocation, and reservation can fail or affect remaining capacity. A configuration that helps a large database can be unnecessary or harmful for a small service.
Inspect rather than prescribe:
grep -E 'Huge|AnonHuge' /proc/meminfo
blocks.title: Original Linux example

blocks.text: Read the workload vendor’s guidance and kernel documentation, measure latency as well as throughput, and include NUMA placement where relevant. Do not enable or disable every huge-page mechanism globally without a tested requirement. (R66)

blocks.text: Beyond basic services, systemd supports sockets, paths, timers, transient units, templates, and relationships among them. Each mechanism changes activation and lifecycle semantics. Socket activation is useful only when the application supports the inherited socket contract or a compatible arrangement.

Template units such as worker@.service allow named instances, but instance values used in paths or commands still need careful escaping and validation. Do not turn an untrusted instance name into a privileged shell command.

Sandbox directives can restrict filesystem access, privileges, and namespaces. Apply them incrementally with application tests. systemd-analyze security can highlight exposure, but its assessment is not a certification that a workload is secure or functionally correct.
Linux example — 30.11
Evaluate an existing unit's isolation settings.
systemd-analyze security nginx.service

blocks.text: Advanced filesystem operations include quotas, reflinks, snapshots, scrubbing, discard, and layout choices where supported. Their availability and semantics vary among ext4, XFS, Btrfs, and other filesystems.

A reflink can share physical extents until data changes; it is not automatically an independent copy for every failure scenario. A scrub can verify selected integrity structures but does not replace all application checks. Discard policy interacts with devices, virtualization, performance, and data-handling requirements.

Start with findmnt and the installed filesystem tools to establish the exact type and features. Never choose a repair or resize command from a different filesystem merely because it has a familiar option name.
Linux example — 30.12
Inspect filesystem type and mount options.

findmnt -o TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS
df -hT

topics.title: 30.13 High-Performance Linux Considerations
topics.summary: High-performance work often balances throughput, tail latency, predictability, and resource cost. CPU isolation, interrupt placement, NUMA policy, storage queues, and network settings can help specific workloads while making general scheduling and maintenance harder.

blocks.text: High-performance work often balances throughput, tail latency, predictability, and resource cost. CPU isolation, interrupt placement, NUMA policy, storage queues, and network settings can help specific workloads while making general scheduling and maintenance harder.

Define the useful unit of work and a correctness check. Measure the latency distribution rather than only the average. A change that improves median response but introduces rare multi-second stalls may violate the real requirement.

Treat tuning as versioned experiments with reproducible inputs. Preserve a supported baseline and remove settings whose benefit is no longer measurable. Complexity without demonstrated value becomes another source of incidents.
Linux example — 30.13
Sample performance with bounded observations.

vmstat 1 3
iostat -xz 1 3
ip -s link

topics.summary: In a disposable VM, protect a small interactive service from an optional batch job. No production workload is involved. First measure both under the same controlled demand. Record the service latency, batch completion time, and host pressure.

blocks.text: In a disposable VM, protect a small interactive service from an optional batch job. No production workload is involved. First measure both under the same controlled demand. Record the service latency, batch completion time, and host pressure.

The simplest intervention is to give the interactive service the highest possible priority. Its limitation is that it can starve other tasks and does not address memory pressure or a shared I/O bottleneck.
